lines.text: 3.9 Food Miles: From the Field to the Plate
Aarav's lunch had rice in it. Ira's had wheat. Neither grew in the school.
Follow a chapati backwards from the plate and you find a chain of work. A farmer
prepares soil, sows wheat, waters and tends it for months, and harvests it. The grain
is threshed and winnowed to separate it from the chaff. It is stored, often for months.
It is transported to a mill and ground into flour. The flour is packed, transported
again, and sold in a shop. Someone buys it, carries it home, kneads it, and cooks
That is many months, many hands, and a great many kilometres, for one item on
The story of a chapati: from field to plate
The total distance a food item travels from producer to consumer is called its
Shorter food miles are better on three counts. Transport costs money and bums fuel,
so a shorter journey means cheaper food and less pollution. Food that travels less
arrives fresher. And buying food grown nearby puts money into the hands of farmers
near you rather than into transport along the way.
